projects.title: a murmuration
projects.lead: Three hundred and thirty feet of wall in Terminal 5, and nearly six hundred convex aluminum discs charting two centuries of immigration to Illinois.
credits: Commissioned by DCASE and the Chicago Department of Aviation
Finishing: EH Schwab, Pioneer Metal, Gatto Metal
body: In the corridors of Chicago's O'Hare International Airport, a sweeping narrative of immigration and diversity unfolds across 330 feet of wall. "a murmuration," conceived by artist Jina Valentine and brought to life by ChiLab Studio, is a piece of data visualization built at architectural scale.

Using census data from 1850 to 2040, the installation translates demographic information into an array of colors and sizes. Nearly 600 convex aluminum discs were crafted, each varying to represent a different immigrant population and period. A color coding system ties each disc's hue to a continent of origin.
Eighty of the discs carry engraved phrases contributed by community partners, in their own languages, on the themes of home, welcome, and community.

Material selection was driven by the environment. Zinc plated steel and anodized aluminum were chosen for durability and finish stability in a high traffic terminal, and the install was sequenced around live airport operations.

story.label: The work
text: Jina Valentine's a murmuration maps more than two centuries of immigration to the region now called Illinois across 330 feet of Terminal 5. Nearly six hundred discs each stand for an immigrant population by decade, sized to Census data and colored by continent of origin. Their arrangement comes from an adaptation of the BOIDS flocking algorithm, the movement of a starling murmuration, and the armatures follow the region's waterways, drawn from an early map narrated by an Indigenous mapmaker laid against a contemporary one. For all the data behind it, what it says to a traveller is simple: welcome.

story.label: The material question
text: Valentine wanted the discs at five different degrees of concavity. A single curvature would have been far cheaper to tool, and it would have flattened the work. The variation was the point, so the tooling had to carry it. Eighty discs also carry phrases of home, welcome, and community, and those had to read the way someone from that place would actually say them, not the way a dictionary would.

story.label: The making
text: Five separate tools, one for each curvature, with production at a volume where every disc still matched its set. Zinc plated steel and anodized aluminum were chosen for durability and finish stability in a high traffic terminal. The engraved phrases came from the artist's team working with embassies around the world to get each language right, down to the informal turns of phrase someone from that land would be used to hearing.

story.label: In place
text: A permanent installation, sequenced around live airport operations. What Valentine and her team did to bring those voices in was remarkable, and we were proud to give them a surface that will last.

projects.title: Grand Spiral Stair
projects.sub: Uber Freight HQ, Old Post Office
projects.lead: A sixteen foot diameter stair finished in a custom blue toned patina, inspired by the building's historical spiral mail chutes.
projects.materials: Fabricated steel, custom blue patina, mirror
body: In the heart of Chicago's Old Post Office, now home to Uber Freight's headquarters, the Grand Spiral Stair is more than vertical circulation. It is a piece of the building's history returned in contemporary form.

The geometry takes its cue from the spiral mail chutes that once moved letters through the building. The finish is a custom blue toned patina that reads close to oil rubbed bronze, and an infinity mirror at the top extends the spiral past the ceiling.
Produced in collaboration with Gensler Chicago, the stair merges art, technology, and function inside a landmark structure.

story.label: The work
text: The Old Post Office once moved letters through spiral mail chutes. The Grand Spiral Stair, at the center of Uber Freight's headquarters, takes its geometry from them. Next to a photograph of the original chutes the reference is obvious. On its own it reads as one spiraling band moving through the building, and that is how most people meet it.

story.label: The material question
text: A sixteen foot helix inside a landmark had to be structure, circulation, and finish at once, and the finish had to belong to a century-old interior rather than sit on top of it.

story.label: The making
text: Fabricated steel, produced with Gensler Chicago and Parenti & Raffaelli, finished in a custom blue toned patina that reads close to oil rubbed bronze. An infinity mirror at the top carries the spiral on past the ceiling.

story.label: In place
text: It was ChiLab's first union job and our first large-scale installation in a historic building, one of two pieces we built for Uber Freight's headquarters.

projects.title: Parametric Feature Wall
projects.sub: Uber Freight HQ, Old Post Office
projects.lead: A cast metal wall derived from the bird's eye view of a shipping yard, modeled parametrically and cast component by component.
body: The wall draws from an unexpected source: the view of a shipping yard from space. The reference ties Uber Freight's mission directly to the architecture of its office.
Using Grasshopper, we built a parametric model tuned to the exact constraints of the space, then sliced the model into individual cast components, each one unique but part of a continuous field.
Mold creation was automated so the volume of unique parts stayed economical, and the castings were finished and assembled on site into a single continuous surface.

story.label: The work
text: The idea came from the team at Gensler Chicago: a freight yard seen from above, containers stacked at varied heights, abstracted into a wall. It ties what Uber Freight does to the room where it does it.

story.label: The material question
text: A field of unique parts. Every panel different, all of them reading as one continuous surface, and all of them draft-free, which conventional patterns cannot give you.

story.label: The making
text: We built a parametric model in Grasshopper tuned to the space, sliced it into individual cast components, and printed the sand molds straight from the digital files, with no pattern in between. Done conventionally it would easily have cost four times as much and still could not have been draft-free; the design was only possible because that technology had just arrived. It was not clean. About eighteen panels came back scaled wrong: measured on site, they had shrunk in casting more than we had allowed for, and every one had to be reordered. A bummer, and a good lesson.

story.label: In place
text: The castings were finished and assembled on site into a single continuous surface, one of two pieces we built for the building.

projects.title: KNOLL Showroom Marquee
projects.lead: Chrome tubes rising from the sixth floor to the seventh floor skylight, with the KNOLL name in dark bronze.
credits: With CNL Projects, Gensler, and KNOLL
body: In Chicago's West Loop, ChiLab produced an architectural sculpture that works as both a functional marquee and a brand statement for the KNOLL showroom.

Chrome tubes arranged in a row soar from the 6th floor to the skylight on the 7th, creating a vertical presence that pulls the eye upward. The KNOLL name is spelled in dark bronze letters mounted to the tubes, tying the screen to the 24 foot bronze table that anchors the showroom floor.
The chrome and bronze palette was chosen against the warm red marble of the entry, so the sculpture reads as part of the room rather than an object placed in it.
The design is a nod to Harry Bertoia, whose work for KNOLL in the 1950s still sets the terms for the company's design language.

story.label: The work
text: The marquee for Knoll's Fulton Market flagship rises from the sixth floor to the skylight on the seventh, a row of chrome tubes with the KNOLL name in dark bronze. Its repeating wireframe is a conscious quote of Harry Bertoia, whose work for Knoll in the 1950s still sets the company's design language, and it was a reference shared between us and the architects at Gensler. Getting to quote that history was an honor.

story.label: The material question
text: Knoll's architects first proposed black pipe. We proposed chrome plated steel, set against the warm red marble of the entry so the piece reads as part of the room rather than an object placed in it. Knoll's directors latched onto it.

story.label: The making
text: Developed through samples in both steel and bronze before approval: roughly 150 custom components and 300 cut and welded caps, built on a fast track of four to five weeks.

story.label: In place
text: The flagship opened in June 2019 and was later featured in Interior Design. For us the marquee is a standalone work of art we got to design and build.

story.label: Also at Fulton Market
text: Alongside the marquee we worked with the designers of Knoll's Antenna table and their manufacturing studio on a 24 foot solid bronze recreation of the table, and made steel handrail covers for the showroom. That work was a collaboration inside an established design. The marquee was ours.

projects.title: Glass Crosses
projects.sub: St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church, National Shrine
projects.lead: Four hundred and twenty hand cast and polished glass crosses set into Pentelic marble doors at the 9/11 Memorial.
projects.materials: Optically clear leaded glass, Pentelic marble
body: St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church sits within the National Shrine at Ground Zero. Taking part in the adornment of a monument with that weight went beyond Chicago or New York and into the national record.

The crosses are cast from a high quality, optically clear leaded glass chosen to capture and refract light. Each one was cast, cold worked, and polished by hand, then set into CNC machined openings in the Pentelic marble doors.
The work demanded technical precision and an understanding of what the crosses would mean once installed.

story.label: The work
text: St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church and National Shrine stands at the World Trade Center site. Santiago Calatrava's building joins Byzantine tradition with contemporary design, and its doors carry four hundred and twenty clear glass crosses set into marble. Transparency lets light pass through. In a sacred site rebuilt after September 11, that is the meaning.

story.label: The material question
text: The marble is from Mount Pentelicus, the quarry that supplied the Parthenon. It has long been closed, and using it requires sanction from both the Greek government and the church. Permission came because this small church had been the founding site of the Greek Orthodox Church in Manhattan. Every cross had to fit stone that cannot be replaced.

story.label: The making
text: Each cross was cast in optically clear leaded glass, cold worked, and polished by hand. Fit was solved in the model. The CNC cut openings in the marble did not match the drawings we had been sent, so we measured the first machined sample, rebuilt our models from the actual stone, and travelled to the site to confirm the openings there matched it. Only then did we produce the run. They all fit.

story.label: In place
text: “It was every craftsman's dream to be able to work on pieces that will last a lifetime in a sacred site,” says Ally Reza. There was reverence and care in each one, and it was an honor to be trusted with those materials and to set our glass within them.

projects.title: Icon Stands
projects.sub: St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church, National Shrine
projects.lead: Matching pairs of bronze pedestals at the chapel entry, engineered with Santiago Calatrava.
projects.materials: Cast and fabricated bronze, Pentelic marble
body: The gravity defying stature of the pedestal design was an engineering problem as much as a design one, resolved in collaboration with Santiago Calatrava.
In matching pairs, the bronze pedestals serve the entryway of the chapel, ordained with iconographic tablets. As guests enter, the pedestals function as bases for prayer.
Contemporary metalworking meets an ancient stone: the pedestals carry Pentelic marble, the same quarry that supplied the Parthenon.

story.label: The work
text: Two pairs of bronze and marble pedestals at the chapel entry, holding icons that are changed through the year with the church's rituals and celebrations. They serve the flow of the service as much as the eye.

story.label: The material question
text: Calatrava wanted the cross form uninterrupted, perfect, and balanced: a gravity defying stance that was an engineering problem as much as a design one. And each stand had to carry Pentelic marble.

story.label: The making
text: Cast and fabricated bronze, engineered with Calatrava's office. We were ten times more careful with that marble than with almost any material we have handled.

story.label: In place
text: The crates the marble shipped in are still with us. We keep them like reliquaries.

projects.title: Illinois State Capitol Handrails
projects.sub: Office of the Architect of the Capitol
projects.lead: Nineteenth century iron handrails on the fourth floor gallery, restored and brought to ADA compliance without losing their period character.
credits: Office of the Architect of the Capitol
body: After removing layers of failing faux paint and documenting dozens of missing or broken ornamental pieces, we digitally modeled replacement components from archival profiles.

New upper ornamental details and toe kick elements were developed as 3D models, then translated into match plate sand patterns with engineered gating. Masters were 3D printed directly into the pattern boards, molded in resin bonded sand, and cast in iron to integrate with the originals.
For repairs to original rail sections, lost wax reproductions of missing details were produced, assembled, and patinated to match the existing finish.
A custom mill worked wooden handrail cap was fitted atop the ironwork, providing both a crown and the height required for ADA compliance.

story.label: The work
text: The fourth floor gallery outside the Illinois House of Representatives is lined with nineteenth century cast iron handrails, bought from a Sears catalog in the late 1890s. Over the decades they had been painted and repainted to look like bronze, then gold, then back again. The job was to return them to what they were, and to make them safe for the people who use the building now.

story.label: The material question
text: Restoration means matching what already exists, and much of it was missing. The railing also had to reach ADA height and gain a toe kick, so nothing is kicked from the fourth floor onto the third, without the additions reading as a violation of the original.

story.label: The making
text: We removed the components and stripped them back to bare iron. The railing is modular and its sections repeat, so a detail missing in one panel could almost always be found in another; we molded just that portion and cast the replacements, alongside match plate sand patterns and lost wax reproductions patinated to match. The original top rail had itself been wood, in very poor condition. We replaced it with a cap milled to the same profile used throughout the capitol, which gave the height ADA required.

story.label: In place
text: For Ben Stagl it was one of the biggest honors of his life. The Architect of the Capitol took him inside the walls and up into the cupola, where they came out at the top with a direct line of sight to Lincoln's tomb. Then he handed Ben a Sharpie and let him sign the inside of the cupola, alongside others who have worked on the building.

projects.title: Flight of Butterflies
projects.lead: Twenty nine cast aluminum butterfly sculptures installed across Chicago, each finished by a local artist.
projects.materials: Cast aluminum, steel, artist applied finishes
body: Flight of Butterflies features 29 uniquely adorned butterfly sculptures installed across Chicago, from Lakeview to South Shore to Austin. Our team designed and crafted the butterflies, providing the foundation for local artists to embellish and bring them to life.

Each butterfly was digitally designed in two motifs, the Regal Fritillary and the Black Swallowtail, then 3D rendered to produce molds for the cast aluminum bodies. Custom CNC cut wood served as the positive for the molds, which kept production controlled given the quantity and the schedule.
Every casting was hand finished to a state that would take paint, so each artist could work directly on the surface.
Where an artist's work had not been built for the outdoors, we supplied material samples and methods that kept their idea intact while making it survive a Chicago year.

story.label: The work
text: Twenty nine six-foot butterflies across Chicago, from Lakeview to South Shore to Austin, each finished by a different local artist, for the Peggy Notebaert Nature Museum. Two species, the Regal Fritillary and the Black Swallowtail, carried out of the museum and into neighborhoods across the city.

story.label: The material question
text: One blank, twenty nine artists, and a year outdoors in Chicago. The sculpture had to be a clean canvas any artist could work on, and survive whatever they put on it.

story.label: The making
text: Bodies modeled in both motifs, rendered into molds, and cast in aluminum on steel bases, every casting hand finished to take paint. Then the studio itself changed: we reconfigured the whole shop and opened a new section so the artists could work on site, and spent most of those months getting them information, materials, and room. Where we had concerns about an artist's materials we raised them through Cortney Lederer of CNL Projects, curator and liaison. Mostly the choice was deliberate, and the artist was right.

story.label: In place
text: Most pieces held up and surprised us. A few showed nature overtaking a medium, where an artist had stepped away from what we recommended. In Lederer's words: “Twenty-nine artists participated and all required different logistical needs and material expertise, and ChiLab delivered.”

projects.title: Tulips on The Magnificent Mile
projects.lead: Five oversized tulip sculptures placed along Michigan Avenue for the city's annual spring bloom.
body: In the spring of 2025, in partnership with The Magnificent Mile Association and CNL Projects, we developed five custom tulip sculptures with artist Aiden Kelley for the city's signature street.
Chicago's annual tulip bloom blankets the Mile with color. These sculptures were an opportunity to put public sculpture and Chicago's floral tradition in the same frame.

Each tulip was installed at a different point along the stretch. The sculpture at 625 N. Michigan Avenue shows the Official Magnificent Mile Tulip in brilliant yellow with orange accents, cultivated specifically for Michigan Avenue's displays and bred to hold up in Chicago's unpredictable spring.

story.label: The work
text: The Apeldoorn tulip was bred in Holland specifically for Chicago's Magnificent Mile, and the Consulate General of the Netherlands took part in baptizing it. For years it could only be found on the Mile. Five oversized tulip sculptures, developed with artist Aiden Kelley, The Magnificent Mile Association, and CNL Projects, put Chicago's signature spring bloom into public sculpture.

story.label: The material question
text: A scaled up flower only works if it reads as the flower. Each tulip had to feel organic and pronounced, like a perfectly scaled up version of the real thing, and its color had to belong to its sponsor: the Apeldoorn's own red and yellow at 625 N. Michigan, and for the Driehaus Museum the exact reverse, yellow tips over red petals.

story.label: The making
text: We dissected tulips to study their build, then fabricated the petals and finished them in automotive paint. Colors were chosen by each sponsoring business on the Mile, and as sponsors have picked new tulip varieties in recent years, the flowerbeds around the sculptures have been planted to match.

story.label: In place
text: A Chicago spring is wet and windy and tests everything left out in it. Every couple of years we collect the petals and repaint them, sometimes just covering dirt, sometimes wear and scratches, so the tulips come back fresh and new looking each season.

projects.title: SKIMS Storefronts
projects.lead: Cast glass logo displays engineered for the brand's first brick and mortar storefronts.
body: In 2024 we developed storefront displays for SKIMS locations across the US. The project was a union of artistic vision and large scale engineering, and it pushed the limits of architectural glass fabrication.
Designed by Willo Perron of Perron-Roettinger Studio, the logo appears to emerge from the storefront window, a sleek effect in keeping with the brand.

Bringing it to life took the combined expertise of Perron-Roettinger Studio, ChiLab Studio, and AGNORA, North America's leader in large format glass. Traditional casting technique met contemporary lamination and structural glazing.

story.label: The work
text: For SKIMS's first brick and mortar stores, Willo Perron of Perron-Roettinger Studio wanted the logo to emerge from the storefront glass. The first premise followed the store's fabrics: soft, voluminous body forms pushing out of the window.

story.label: The material question
text: Soft forms projecting from glass are hard to make and could not hold the fidelity of the logo. So the question became whether thick glass castings could be laminated to oversized architectural windows. As far as anyone knew, it had not been done.

story.label: The making
text: We cast the logo; AGNORA, North America's large format glass specialist, laminated it to the storefront glass. Both sides had a good feeling about it, and until the prototype came through the process we were all holding our breath. We saw it at AGNORA's facility in Canada, beside the largest autoclave we had ever seen and a 32 foot conference table made from a single sheet of glass.

story.label: In place
text: The castings read as prismatic lenses. Walking up, you see into the store as if through a galaxy. A first of its kind, in Miami, Atlanta, and Houston.

projects.title: Jardin de Gargolas
projects.lead: Student designed garden gargoyles taken from 3D model to cast aluminum sculpture.
body: In collaboration with YolloCalli Arts Reach and artist educator Secret of Manna, we helped bring students' 3D digital garden gargoyle designs into the physical world.

Starting in fall 2023, students conceptualized their creations in design software. By spring the project had become a fabrication and exhibition class. We printed the sculptures in house and prepared them for casting.
The 3D printed sculptures became the positive for a resin sand mold system, a lost PLA process that gives a direct translation between the digital design and its metal duplicate.
Once cast, the gargoyle pieces were welded together and finished with a dark patina.

story.label: The work
text: Little Village teens with Yollocalli Arts Reach, the youth art program of the National Museum of Mexican Art, designed their own garden gargoyles in 3D software, with artist Secret of Manna. The idea grew from a rainwater garden and a bird bath, and the gargoyles are destined for Jardin Malinalli, the museum's youth garden in Pilsen and Little Village.

story.label: The material question
text: A file on a screen had to become a permanent metal object, true to what each student made, and the students had to understand the process well enough to design for it.

story.label: The making
text: The class came to the shop first. We showed them how their 3D prints would become molds and how metal would be poured, and poured a tiny demonstration mold that day. What they brought back for the real pour was really impressive. We printed the sculptures in house as positives for a resin bonded sand mold, a lost PLA process, then cast in aluminum, welded, and finished in a dark patina. We cast one early for a big reveal: everyone had seen the prints, but seeing it in metal was something else. The rest took about a week to cast.

story.label: In place
text: Unveiled in April 2024 in the museum courtyard, part of the exhibition New Age Grotesque. Each gargoyle sat on its own pedestal in a small garden of flowers, each given its own space and all displayed as equals.

projects.title: Homebound
projects.lead: A CNC cut aluminum collage in Grant Park, built to survive a Chicago spring.
body: In the spring of 2023 we collaborated with Chicago based photographer Leonard Suryajaya on Homebound, a public land art installation at the northern end of the Grant Park waterfront trail. Homebound was one of twelve pieces supported by the E(art)h Chicago collective and installed in neighborhoods across the city.

Mirroring the collage language of Suryajaya's photographs, we used CNC cut aluminum panels pieced together as a three dimensional puzzle, translating work he had previously made in wrapped and layered materials into something that could live outdoors.
The formation takes the shape of a Maneki-Neko, the lucky cat, surrounded by silhouettes of fruit, reading as a dismantled fruit stand and referencing the artist's upbringing in Indonesia.

story.label: The work
text: Leonard Suryajaya called it a memorial to our relationship with earth as home. The piece takes its shape from the Maneki-Neko, the lucky cat, and from the deconstructed forms of roadside fruit stands. Three heads emerge from the ground framing the sun path, the lake, and the river, with fruits in disguise scattered around the base like offerings on an altar. It is adorned with familiar eyes and photographic artifacts from the artist's home in Chicago and his hometown in Indonesia.

story.label: The material question
text: Suryajaya's collages are paper, layered and cut. This one had to stand on the lakefront through a Chicago spring and still read as collage: the eyes legible up close, the layering legible at monument scale, the images surviving wind, sun, and weather for a season outdoors. The problem was carrying a paper language into a material that does not behave like paper.

story.label: The making
text: We translated the artist's forms into buildable drawings, then CNC cut aluminum sheet and formed it into the heads and the fruit, pieced together as a three dimensional puzzle. Parts were welded and finished for an outdoor site, and the eyes and photographic artifacts were printed across the aluminum surface so the collage lived in the metal rather than on top of it.

story.label: In place
text: Installed on the lakefront at the north end of the Grant Park waterfront trail, one of twelve pieces supported by E(art)h Chicago across the city. It was an honor to work with a Chicago artist, to build community around this city, and to help bring his work into civic space. We worked with Suryajaya twice over two years, on Homebound and again on Flight of Butterflies.

projects.title: St. Alfred
projects.lead: A powder coated steel fixture system and stone topped cash counter for the Chicago streetwear boutique.
body: A custom retail fixture and display package for Saint Alfred, produced with Chelsea Lombardo of Interiors + Objects.

We translated the retail design into a single powder coated steel system: display fixtures, modified industrial shelving, shoe racks, hanger bars, and a modular center display, with a steel clad cash counter topped in stone.

story.label: The work
text: Saint Alfred is a Chicago streetwear boutique. For its flagship, Chelsea Lombardo designed a store that would read as one room: every fixture part of the same object rather than a collection of furniture.

story.label: The material question
text: One language across everything. Custom pieces and bought ones had to become indistinguishable, so the whole room would read as a single, specific monochrome.

story.label: The making
text: We translated the retail design into shop drawings and a single steel fixture system: display fixtures, modified industrial shelving, custom shoe racks, hanger bars, and a modular center display, with a steel clad cash counter topped in stone as the anchor of the floor. Everything we fabricated was powder coated, and the parts we bought, down to the shelving used for the clothing racks, were sent out for the same powder coat.

story.label: In place
text: Coordinated around an active construction schedule and assembled on site. A fantastic collaboration with Chelsea Lombardo, with lighting designed and built by Max Davis.

projects.title: Methodology Table
projects.sub: Solid cast glass end table, ongoing since 2016
projects.lead: A solid cast glass end table, produced in an ongoing series for a private client.
body: Solid cast glass end table for a private client. An ongoing fabrication relationship running from 2016 to the present.

story.label: The work
text: A solid cast glass end table for a private client. We had never seen a solid cast glass table like it, and the reason to make it, for us and for the client, was to do something that seems impossible. That is how people take it when they see it in person.

story.label: The material question
text: Glass that thick has to come down in temperature slowly or it cracks. The table runs from thick to thin, two inches at its heaviest, and every section has to cool at the pace of the thickest.

story.label: The making
text: We anneal as if it were twice as thick as it is. Each table spends about ten days in the kiln, nearly a week of that annealing alone. Once the first prototype was dialed in, it rarely fails in the kiln; the risk is in finishing, when it goes back up in temperature for its fine polish.

story.label: In place
text: Ten years on, roughly ten tables. The form stays consistent; the flow of the glass and its bubble pattern are each table's own.

projects.title: 360 N Green Reception
projects.lead: Reception desk for Sterling Bay at 360 N Green.
body: Reception desk at 360 N Green for Sterling Bay. Industrial design, architecture, and interior detailing carried through a single fabricated element.

story.label: The work
text: A reception desk for Sterling Bay at 360 N Green, meant to read as smooth, aged, and modern at once. The whole underside of the desk curves inward, so it seems to float: you almost feel the pebble could roll away, and it doesn't. It sits balanced, and tells you the building is intentional and here for a reason.

story.label: The material question
text: A form that depends on looking effortless. Any flaw in the surface, any seam or dent, would break the sense of a single smooth stone.

story.label: The making
text: Industrial design, architecture, and interior detailing carried through one fabricated element. End pieces made by another shop came in with pour dents, and we concealed them until they matched the consistency and smoothness of everything else. The patina was applied on site, a finish developed for this desk.

story.label: In place
text: Applying a finish we had made up, in place, with no way to take it back to the shop, took a lot of confidence from the whole team. It is one of the details we are proudest of.

projects.title: Pritzker Group Reception Desk
projects.lead: Bronze clad reception desk and bronze framed credenza for the Pritzker Group offices.
credits: With Imperial Woodworking and Lazuli Studio
body: Bronze clad reception desk and bronze framed credenza created for the Pritzker Group offices in Chicago. Developed and executed by ChiLab in collaboration with Imperial Woodworking and Lazuli Studio at the direction of Gensler.

story.label: The work
text: A bronze clad reception desk and bronze framed credenza for the Pritzker Group offices. Bronze is a little bit of a power play, a statement of refined sensibility, and for a financial firm it balances old and new: set against the bright red feature wall behind it, the desk asserts value and taste while staying clean, welcoming, even fun.

story.label: The material question
text: Cladding a desk in bronze leaves no room for error. The seams have to be tight and precise, and the metal has to meet a body built by someone else.

story.label: The making
text: Developed with Imperial Woodworking and Lazuli Studio under Gensler's direction. We had the desk body in our shop while we prepared the cladding, and that is the only reason the work could be so precise: shims glued in at every gap so every measurement held, and some bronze pieces hand cut and beveled on the table saw by Ben Stagl to make the fit.

story.label: In place
text: Installing the cladding on a busy union site, as a small specialist team not used to working that way, was its own challenge. The precision done in the shop is what made it go in clean.

projects.title: Solid Cast Bronze Unfolding Chair
projects.sub: One hundred pounds of solid bronze
projects.lead: The 1941 Krueger steel folding chair, cast solid in bronze and stripped of its ability to fold.
credits: With Bo Rodda, Jason Gillette, Max Davis, Kuan Wen Chiu
body: The Unfolding Chair takes a second look at what might be the most common chair ever made. The 1941 steel folding chair by Krueger Metal Products was designed for utility and economy, made from excess metal from steel companies, light enough to fold and nest, and commonly sold for two dollars.
By producing the image of that chair in solid bronze and removing its ability to fold and nest, the design trades functional value for material value, thus unfolding the design.
Exhibited at WANTED DESIGN NYC in the Chicagoland presentation.

story.label: The work
text: The 1941 Krueger steel folding chair may be the most common chair ever made: about two dollars, made from excess steel, built to fold flat and nest by the hundred, the gym assembly chair kept in high school closets. Its utility made it universal, and it never got the Eames level respect. The Unfolding Chair takes a second look at it.

story.label: The material question
text: To unfold the design is to undo the mechanism that defined it. Recast in a hundred pounds of solid bronze, the chair trades functional value for material value.

story.label: The making
text: The idea came out of a heated debate between Ben Stagl, Bo Rodda, Max Davis, Kuan Wen Chiu, and Jason Gillette about what to take to New York. In a kitchen, someone pointed at a folding chair and said, let's just make that in solid bronze. Who said it is still debated. Ben was running a bronze manufacturing business at the time and saw it immediately: two or three molds, manageable in the time frame.

story.label: In place
text: What no one anticipated was the weight, and how much it would change the experience. On the first day of WANTED DESIGN 2013, in an area curated by Cappellini, he went to move what he thought was a standard folding chair and could not lift it. He stepped back and laughed. The chair went on to the cover of the New York Times' Design Week coverage that year.

projects.title: The Boolean Lamp and Pendant
projects.lead: A hand blown pendant and table lamp, shaped by subtracting the aluminum clip light from a bubble of glass.
body: A lamp and pendant family developed in house, taking its geometry from the boolean intersection of two primitive volumes. Produced in hand blown glass and later scaled into the Kuma's West Loop interior.

story.label: The work
text: The Boolean Lamp starts from the ubiquitous aluminum clip light, the work light in every shop, and looks for luxury in the everyday.

story.label: The material question
text: The name is the method. The lamp's shape is a boolean: the clip light subtracted from a bubble of glass, so the interior of the shade is determined by the exterior of the original aluminum light. The two are connected in lineage, and the glass had to carry that exact geometry.

story.label: The making
text: Each one is blown by glass artisans in Chicago, one at a time, the result of an iterative design process. Variations in color, texture, and shape make each lamp its own within a consistent form. Glass in smoke, umber, or light blue, on a base of cast concrete, aluminum, or acrylic, as a pendant or a table lamp.

story.label: In place
text: Our best selling object to date, sold to businesses overseas and at home and into many luxury kitchens and homes. The pendant also scaled up into the Kuma's Corner West Loop interior, circling the bar.

projects.title: Architizer A+ Award
projects.lead: Award objects for the best architecture built that year, sculpted with Snarkitecture and produced, precisely, hundreds of times.
body: The Architizer A+ Awards trophy, designed by Snarkitecture as a cast block with a torn upper edge and a cross shaped plaque set into the top. The objects were developed with Snarkitecture and produced in series for the 2015 and 2016 programs.

The torn upper edge is the whole design, and holding it identical across a long production run was the problem: a master worked until the fracture read right from every angle, silicone molds that would not soften it, a cultured marble mix that filled it cleanly, and the plaques, packing, and labelling for awards shipping to winners worldwide.

story.label: The work
text: Architizer's A+ Awards name the best architecture built that year, worldwide. Snarkitecture designed the trophy as a cast block with a torn upper edge and a cross shaped plaque set into the top. An object that stands for the best work in architecture has to survive the comparison, and every winner takes one home, so each piece ends up in the house of someone who spends their working life judging how things are made. That is a humbling audience, and it set the standard.

story.label: The material question
text: The torn edge carries the whole idea, and a torn edge is a sculptor's problem, not a machinist's. It had to look broken and feel deliberate. It also had to be the same break, in the same place, on every piece, because a fracture that varies reads as a defect rather than a decision. Cultured marble was the material that could hold a fracture that sharp and still cure to a consistent color.

story.label: The making
text: We worked the master until the break read right from every angle, then built the tooling around protecting exactly that: silicone molds that would survive a long production run without softening the edge, a mix that filled the fracture cleanly, and anodized aluminum plaques set flush into the top.

story.label: Doing it hundreds of times
text: Then the daunting part. Precision once is craft; precision hundreds of times is process. Packing and labelling for awards shipping to winners worldwide, so the last one out the door arrived as sharp as the first.

projects.title: Cast Aluminum Tessellation Wall
projects.lead: A cast aluminum relief wall built from a repeating tile, developed for Gary Lee Partners.
credits: Developed and fabricated by Ben Stagl
body: A relief wall running the length of the counter in a Gary Lee Partners interior, made as a tessellation so that one repeating cast tile could cover the full run without reading as a grid. The tile was modeled digitally, cast in aluminum, then finished and patinated by hand.

Working from a single repeating unit kept tooling and lead time in check at architectural scale. It is an early version of the approach the studio later brought to the parametric cast feature wall at Uber Freight.

story.label: The work
text: A relief wall running the length of the counter in a Gary Lee Partners interior. The design the client had committed to was bronze in the renderings, a rippling surface that should never visibly repeat.

story.label: The material question
text: The price had been promised before the wall was solved. Bronze at that scale, with that many unique pieces, was not possible for it. The question became how to keep the sense of a non-repeating ripple using a limited amount of tooling and a lighter metal.

story.label: The making
text: The answer was tessellation and edge symmetry: one repeating cast aluminum tile that reads as a continuous ripple rather than a grid. It was also the first time we turned aluminum into an oil rubbed bronze finish, and the hand rubbed patina added to the illusion in the best way. It bridged Ben Stagl's early training in patina at art foundries with his new work in Chicago as a designer and bespoke fabricator.

story.label: In place
text: The patina trick became a studio method. We used it again, years later, on the parametric cast feature wall at Uber Freight's headquarters.

projects.title: Kuma's Corner West Loop
projects.lead: Custom lighting, metalwork, furnishings, and artistic details for the Fulton Market location.
projects.materials: Hand blown glass, rusted steel, LED
body: Development and manufacture of custom lighting, metalwork, selected furnishings, and artistic details for the Kuma's Corner West Loop location at Peoria and Fulton Market.

Hand blown Boolean pendants and custom below bar shadow boxes encircle the bar, with five larger Boolean pendants produced for the west wall portals. The below bar LED shadow boxes carry a rusted steel patina.

story.label: The work
text: Custom lighting, metalwork, furnishings, and artistic details for Kuma's Corner at Peoria and Fulton Market. Kuma's has a real culture, and the point was to keep it authentic and at the forefront rather than contrive a theme.

story.label: The material question
text: A franchise opening new locations needs coherent signature elements. The risk is that coherence turns into a theme restaurant. The honesty at Kuma's is the people who work there, so their hands had to be in the room.

story.label: The making
text: Employees contributed their own illustrations and panels, which we built into the bar itself. With one of the cooks, an incredible filigree illustrator, we developed stained glass windows from his drawings, made with our friend Steven Krejcik. Hand blown Boolean pendants circle the bar, with larger ones in the west wall portals, and below bar lights and a stage truss for the hanging bar shelves give the location its signature look.

story.label: In place
text: The coherent pieces carry from location to location. What makes it Kuma's is the culture itself, and the layers the people working there added over the top of it.

projects.title: Jail Debris
projects.lead: Twenty three cast lead crystal bars and bricks taken from a demolished Chicago corrections facility.
body: Rubber molds were taken from bars and bricks salvaged from a demolished Chicago corrections facility, then cast in lead crystal and polished on selected faces. Twenty three elements in total, produced for artist Maria Gaspar.

story.label: The work
text: Maria Gaspar's work centers on incarceration. When a Chicago corrections facility was demolished, she collected bars and bricks from it and wanted to give them a new life. Cast in clear lead crystal, objects that were dense, opaque, and heavy with their history let light through and tell their story differently.

story.label: The material question
text: The originals were not to be cleaned up. The bars carried years of paint, layered in steps, one coat for each era that passed. The bricks are porous. Both had to be molded without stripping that history away or letting it bond to the rubber.

story.label: The making
text: We sealed every piece with a natural, water-soluble coating that held the paint and patina in place and kept them clear of the mold, took rubber molds, and cast them in lead crystal, polished on selected faces.

story.label: In place
text: “It was eerie to think of their previous lives, where they were, what they held, who they held,” says Ally Reza. “Because it's not really what they held so much as what humans used them to hold.” The work asked for reverence, and care.

projects.title: Apple
projects.lead: A cast glass apple, molded from a freshly bitten one.
body: A rubber mold was taken from a freshly bitten apple, capturing the moment and the texture of the bite, then cast in glass for the artist collective Industry of the Ordinary.

story.label: The work
text: A freshly bitten apple, cast in glass for the artist collective Industry of the Ordinary and a private collector with a personal connection to the artists. It holds a single moment.

story.label: The material question
text: An apple browns in minutes. The bite had to be captured before the moment was gone.

story.label: The making
text: The day was scheduled like an organ transfer. The bite was taken with the collector, the apple went straight into a bag and across the city to the studio, where a flask sized to it and the rubber were ready to pour. There was almost no browning. The teeth marks look as if they just happened, and the mold smelled of fresh apple.

story.label: In place
text: We worked with Industry of the Ordinary again a few months later, at the Driehaus Museum.

projects.title: Star Award
projects.lead: A cast lead crystal star for the USFL's season MVP, hand polished, masked, and etched.
body: Cast lead crystal star form produced as an MVP award. Hand polished, masked, and etched.

story.label: The work
text: The MVP award for a season of the USFL. One of the finest awards someone could receive, and it had to look it.

story.label: The material question
text: A star in lead crystal, fully polished, with fine etched detail across its faces, on a silver base.

story.label: The making
text: We made two. Polishing every surface of a star form is its own challenge; masking and etching intricate detail across those polished faces is another.

story.label: In place
text: The league sent a driver with a briefcase built to hand carry it to the game. When the case was opened at the other end, the star had shattered. We still have the photographs.

projects.title: Woven Vessels
projects.lead: Cast lead crystal vessels molded from the artist's earthenware originals.
body: Rubber molds were taken from Candone Wharton's earthenware sculptures and translated into cast lead crystal, carrying the woven surface of the original into a transparent material.

story.label: The work
text: Candone Wharton works in ceramic, black earthenware and sometimes terracotta. Her vessels look woven but are ceramic, and she wanted to see pieces she had loved for a long time come to life in a new material and a new palette: purples, lime greens, jades.

story.label: The material question
text: Something woven, made to let light through. Turning an opaque ceramic translucent gives the piece a second life in its shadows and lets it glow from within, but only if the weave survives the mold.

story.label: The making
text: As mold makers we preserve originals wherever we can. The earthenware got the same natural water-soluble sealer as Maria Gaspar's Jail Debris; we molded it and cast in lead crystal, and the originals came back intact for her to show.

story.label: In place
text: “There's a lot of optical spice in the combination of something woven and then allowing light to pass through it,” says Ally Reza.

projects.title: Annular Sconce
projects.lead: A thirty inch diameter sconce in fused glass and hammered bronze.
body: Fused glass and hammered bronze sconce, 30 inch diameter by 3 inch deep.

story.label: The work
text: Annular maps the full calendar year of 2019 as the planets of our solar system travel through it. An underlying grid reads as the calendar, and lines of air trace the planets' paths. It is rational and specific, and from a step back it is simply calming: a subtle glow, a slow circular motion, a place to sit.

story.label: The material question
text: A year of planetary motion had to read as a map, and as a sky.

story.label: The making
text: In fused glass, the lines we drew to trap air sit among bubbles already in the glass, a starfield the planetary paths are in dialogue with. The hammered bronze is the sun. It blocks the light source, and the light that escapes around it makes a corona across the field.

story.label: In place
text: In the studio's collection, a one-off and the first of a series. The map dictates the period, so the series stays open: other years, and smaller periods at smaller scales.
